from_notes: - **Pioneers of PIL**: **Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer and Justice P.N. Bhagwati** – the first SC judges to admit PILs; with O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai they laid the foundation of activism. Judge "who introduced PIL" = **P.N. Bhagwati**.
dispute: Most books and keys (UPSC 2006): P.N. Bhagwati, the judge who introduced PIL. Strictly: when the first PILs were admitted (1979-81) the CJI was Y.V. Chandrachud (1978-85); Bhagwati was CJI only in 1985-86 (sci.gov.in former CJIs list).
x: P.N. Bhagwati (with V.R. Krishna Iyer) introduced PIL and later became CJI (1985-86), which is why UPSC keyed him. Hidayatullah (1968-70), Ahmadi (1994-97) and Anand (1998-2001) had nothing to do with PIL's start.

from_notes: - **PIL = outcome of judicial activism** (its most popular form) – not of judicial restraint; "intertwined with" activism.
x: PIL is the most popular form and outcome of judicial activism, which began in India in the mid-1970s. Judicial review is the basis of activism, not the thing activism is 'related to' in this standard question.

from_notes: - PIL under **Art. 32 (SC)** or **Art. 226 (HC)**; in line with **Art. 39A**.
x: A PIL can be filed in the Supreme Court under Art. 32 or in a High Court under Art. 226. Tribunals such as the CAT are not PIL forums.

from_notes: - **Judicial activism**: originated in the **USA**; term coined **1947** by **Arthur Schlesinger Jr.**; in India from the **mid-1970s** (post-Emergency). PIL: originated in the **USA in the 1960s**; in India early **1980s** (first cases 1979).
x: PIL originated in the USA in the 1960s and came to India in the late 1970s / early 1980s. England, Russia and China are wrong.

from_notes: - **Overreach**: courts entering the executive / legislative domain → strains (blurs) **separation of powers**.
x: Judicial overreach is when activism goes beyond limits and the judiciary encroaches on the domain of the executive and legislature. Options 1 and 4 describe ordinary judicial review; option 2 describes only one form of activism.
